title: Recovery: why the log must come first
lead: A successful commit and a written data page are different events. We will keep RAM, disk and the durable log in separate columns, so a crash reveals exactly what must be reconstructed and what must be removed.
goals: Derive UNDO and REDO requirements from the buffer policy
Apply the two mandatory WAL ordering rules
Follow the analysis, redo, and undo phases

sections.title: Why memory and disk can disagree
sections.html:
Recall the buffer pool: the DBMS edits a page in RAM, then eventually writes that page to storage. A changed page whose stored copy has not caught up is dirty. A flush writes a buffered page to durable storage. A power failure removes RAM, not the surviving disk copy in this lesson's crash model.

Suppose A was 12. T1 changes it to 10 in RAM and commits, but its page has not been flushed. After a crash disk still says 12. Keeping a commit requires reconstructing the new value: REDO. Now suppose B was 7. Uncommitted T2 changes it to 3 and its page is flushed. If T2 aborts, disk must go back to 7: UNDO.

These situations follow from two independent buffer-policy choices:

Policy questionChoiceRecovery consequence
May a page with an uncommitted update be flushed to free its frame?STEAL: yes; NO-STEAL: noSTEAL needs UNDO support
Must every changed data page be flushed before commit?FORCE: yes; NO-FORCE: noNO-FORCE needs REDO support

Thus STEAL+NO-FORCE needs both directions. It makes normal operation flexible: a full buffer can evict dirty pages, and commit need not wait for scattered data-page writes. The cost is recovery machinery and a durable record of changes.

NO-STEAL+FORCE reduces these two recovery needs, but uncommitted pages must fit in memory and commit writes may be expensive. Those policy names alone do not make a multi-page flush atomic: a crash halfway through still needs a correct completion/rollback mechanism.

Key takeaway

STEAL requires UNDO support; NO-FORCE requires REDO support. These requirements arise because a data page may reach disk at a different time from its transaction's commit.

Under NO-STEAL+NO-FORCE, which recovery direction is needed after a crash?

Worked answer. REDO for committed pages that never reached disk. NO-STEAL prevents unfinished updates reaching disk, so these policy choices do not require disk UNDO for them. This answer concerns the stated crash and buffer model, not every possible failure.

sections.title: Separate the page state from the transaction outcome
sections.html:
Original two-product example: data pages A and B are separate; initial disk values are A=12, B=7. The following legal STEAL+NO-FORCE trace also assumes the required log records have been made durable before page writes.

StepRAM valuesDisk valuesDurable log evidence
012,712,7Empty
1: T1 changes A10,712,7T1: A 12→10
2: T1 commits10,712,7Also T1 COMMIT
3: T2 changes B10,312,7Also T2: B 7→3
4: flush B10,312,3No T2 COMMIT
5: crashLost12,3All listed records survive

A's page is old despite its committed transaction. B's page is new despite its uncommitted transaction. The disk values alone cannot tell you which changes belong in the final database. The log supplies both outcome and change information.

At restart, reconstruct T1's A=10 and remove T2's B=3 by restoring B=7. Final data is A=10, B=7. Merely retaining all stored pages leaves both objects wrong. Merely replaying all updates leaves B wrong. Merely restoring all old values discards T1's acknowledged work.

A log entry such as T2: B 7→3 carries old information for undo and new information for redo in this simplified physical-update example. Real records can use more specific change descriptions. Log records are small and appended sequentially, so making the log durable can be cheaper than immediately writing every data page.

Change the trace: neither data page was flushed. What are the disk state after the crash and the desired final state?

Worked answer. Disk is A=12,B=7. The desired final state is still A=10,B=7, because T1 committed and T2 did not. A needs reconstruction; B already has its final value, although an ARIES history-redo phase may temporarily apply T2 before undoing it.

sections.title: Make the evidence durable before relying on it
sections.html:
The previous trace assumed a surviving log. Why must its timing be controlled? Suppose the DBMS first writes uncommitted B=3 to disk, while the only record of old B=7 remains in RAM. Crash now: RAM disappears, and recovery knows neither that 3 is unfinished nor how to restore 7.

Write-ahead logging (WAL) closes that window. The relevant update records must reach durable storage before their updated data page reaches durable storage. Editing a page and staging a log record in RAM may happen earlier; “log first” refers to the required persistence order.

A second window concerns the application's success message. If the update log is durable but COMMIT exists only in RAM, the user could see success and then restart into a system with no durable evidence of success. Therefore the transaction's log through COMMIT must be durable before acknowledging commit.

BoundaryMust already be durableNeed all data pages be durable?
Flush updated B pageThe recovery log records for that pageThis boundary concerns B
Tell T1 that commit succeededT1 log through COMMITNo, under NO-FORCE

Return to A 12→10: stage the update, flush the log, append/flush COMMIT, then acknowledge. The data page may still say 12 on disk. A crash loses RAM but the log rebuilds 10. Alternatively, a page can be flushed before commit if its log is durable; that is why undo information matters under STEAL.

These are ordering requirements, not an instruction to flush a whole log file separately for every changed row. Batching durable log writes can serve several updates while respecting both boundaries.

Key takeaway

WAL does not require every data page to be on disk at commit. Under NO-FORCE, a durable log provides the information needed for REDO after a crash. A COMMIT record present only in RAM is insufficient for reporting success.

The B update record is durable, but T2 COMMIT is not. May B be flushed? May commit success be acknowledged?

Worked answer. B may be flushed under STEAL because its recovery record survives. Success may not yet be acknowledged because the log through COMMIT is not durable. The two WAL boundaries deliberately have different conditions.

sections.title: Rebuild the crash history, then remove unfinished work
sections.html:
The ARIES introduction uses STEAL+NO-FORCE and WAL. Its phases separate finding recovery work from doing that work. Use the changed trace where neither page was flushed. Disk is A=12,B=7; durable log is LSN 10: T1 A 12→10; LSN 20: T2 B 7→3; LSN 30: T1 COMMIT. An LSN is a log sequence number identifying a record's position.

PhaseWhat it learns or appliesExample data state
AnalysisFind active transactions and potentially dirty pages; T1 committed, T2 unfinishedDisk starts 12,7
RedoRepeat required history, including updates of transactions that will abortA=10,B=3
UndoReverse T2’s unfinished updateA=10,B=7

Calling committed T1 a winner and unfinished T2 a loser summarizes their ordinary single-node outcomes. It does not mean redo ignores T2. The intermediate B=3 state is intentional; the final state excludes it. A full implementation tests which logged actions are already reflected on each page instead of blindly applying every record.

Optional: where to start and how to survive another crash

A checkpoint records recovery bookkeeping. Analysis uses checkpoint information and scans forward; redo can need an older update to a page still dirty at the checkpoint. A page's pageLSN identifies its latest applied update. A checkpoint is therefore not a blanket instruction to discard all earlier redo work.

Beyond the core slides, ARIES records undo as a compensation log record (CLR). Original example: a transaction writes A 5→8 at LSN 10, B 9→4 at LSN 20. Rollback restores B=9 and durably records CLR 30 with undoNextLSN=10. Crash again before B's restoration reaches disk. Redo CLR 30 to restore B=9, then resume undo at 10 to restore A=5. A CLR is redoable, is not itself undone, and avoids compensating LSN 20 twice. This illustrates the purpose, not the complete ARIES algorithm.

Forward connection to Lecture 22: a distributed participant with durable PREPARE but no local COMMIT is in doubt, not an ordinary loser. Its global decision must first be resolved before local recovery chooses its outcome.

In the no-flush example, why is B=3 after redo not a recovery error?

Worked answer. Redo reconstructs required history, so T2 may temporarily reappear. Recovery is incomplete at that point. Undo then removes T2 and restores B=7. Judge the final result after all required phases, not the intermediate redo image.

sections.title: Ask which evidence survives the failure
sections.html:
The whole argument depends on surviving evidence. A constraint violation or deadlock may abort one transaction while the DBMS keeps running. A system crash, such as power loss, removes volatile state; this lesson assumes stable storage remains intact. A media failure can instead destroy stored data or the log itself.

If both the data disk and log disk are destroyed, their log records cannot reconstruct anything. Recover from an appropriate surviving backup or replica outside that failure domain. Replication is only helpful for that scenario if the other copy actually survives and contains usable recovery information.

When analyzing any recovery proposal, write down four things: transaction outcome, durable log prefix, durable page contents, and the failure assumption. For an update 20→15, undo restores 20; redo reinstates 15. The current number on disk does not identify which direction is correct. A committed transaction may need redo because its page is old; an unfinished one may need undo because its page is new.

The recovery lab is a small WAL/REDO/UNDO model, not a full ARIES implementation. Use it to predict a final state before running the trace. When reading a production recovery algorithm, additionally check its page tests, transaction chains, checkpoints, compensation records and treatment of in-doubt distributed participants.

Disk has A=15 after update 20→15. Does that prove the transaction committed?

Worked answer. No. STEAL permits an unfinished update to reach disk. Consult durable outcome evidence: committed work should survive, while ordinary aborted/unfinished work must be removed under the recovery protocol. If the log is also destroyed, this crash-recovery argument cannot supply the missing evidence.

quiz.question: What does STEAL + NO-FORCE typically require?
quiz.explanation: STEAL can put uncommitted data on disk, while NO-FORCE can leave committed data only in RAM.

source.summary: Lecture 21 connects buffer policies to recovery, explains WAL, and introduces the three ARIES phases: analysis, redo, and undo.

limitations: The lecture introduces ARIES at a high level; it is not a complete implementation specification.
